meta.titre: Electromagnetic induction: from moving magnets to transformers
meta.sous_theme: Faraday's law, Lenz's law, generators and transformers

sections.contenu_markdown: The electricity in a house in Limbe is produced far away at a dam or a power station, then travels along cables on tall pylons before it is reduced to $220\,\mathrm{V}$ near the homes. Two ideas from one discovery make this possible: a changing magnetic field can create a voltage, and this voltage can be raised or lowered with a transformer. Questions on induction appear in every GCE paper: to explain what is observed when a magnet moves near a coil, to calculate the voltage and current of a transformer, and to explain why a.c. is used.

items: A magnet has a magnetic field around it; field lines go from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.
A coil is a conductor wound in many turns; a galvanometer detects small currents.
Electrical power is $P = IV$, and the energy lost as heat in a wire is larger for a larger current.

sections.titre: Induced e.m.f., Lenz's law and the transformer
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Electromagnetic induction** is the production of an e.m.f. in a conductor when the magnetic field linking it changes, that is, when the conductor cuts magnetic field lines. If the circuit is closed, an induced current flows.

**Faraday's law.** The induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate at which the magnetic field lines are cut (the rate of change of magnetic flux). The e.m.f. is larger if (i) the magnet or the coil moves faster, (ii) the magnet is stronger, (iii) the coil has more turns. If the magnet is stationary, nothing is induced.

**Lenz's law.** The direction of the induced current is such that its magnetic effect opposes the change that produces it. When a north pole is pushed into a coil, the end of the coil nearest the magnet becomes a north pole and repels the magnet. This is a consequence of the conservation of energy: the work done against the repulsion is what supplies the electrical energy.

**The transformer** has two coils (the primary and the secondary) wound on a laminated soft iron core. An alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic field in the core, which induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary:

$$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}$$

For an ideal transformer there is no loss of power, so $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$. In a real one, efficiency $= \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_pI_p} \times 100\%$. A step-up transformer has $N_s > N_p$ (more voltage, less current); a step-down transformer has $N_s < N_p$.

A transformer works **only with a.c.**: with d.c. the field in the core is steady, so no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary. The core is made of soft iron because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised, and it is laminated (thin insulated sheets) to reduce eddy currents that heat the core.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a question asks how electricity is produced by rotation
variantes.contenu_markdown: A coil rotating in a magnetic field cuts the field lines and an alternating e.m.f. is induced. Slip rings and carbon brushes connect the rotating coil to the external circuit. The e.m.f. is larger for faster rotation, a stronger field, more turns or a larger coil. The direction of the induced current in a moving wire is given by Fleming's right-hand rule: the thumb gives the motion, the first finger gives the field, and the second finger gives the current.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked why power is transmitted at high voltage
variantes.contenu_markdown: For a given power $P = IV$, a high voltage means a small current. The power wasted as heat in the cables is $I^2R$, so a small current gives a very small loss. For example, sending $20\,\mathrm{kW}$ along cables of resistance $0.5\,\Omega$ at $400\,\mathrm{V}$ requires $50\,\mathrm{A}$ and wastes $50^2 \times 0.5 = 1250\,\mathrm{W}$ ($6.25\%$). At $20\,000\,\mathrm{V}$ the current is $1.0\,\mathrm{A}$ and the loss is $0.5\,\mathrm{W}$. A step-up transformer at the power station and step-down transformers near the users make this possible, which is why a.c. is used.

variantes.nom: Observations with a magnet and a coil
variantes.quand_utiliser: when a magnet is moved towards, away from, or kept still near a coil
variantes.contenu_markdown: Magnet moving in: the galvanometer deflects one way. Magnet moving out: it deflects the other way. Magnet at rest in or near the coil: no deflection. Faster movement: a larger deflection. More turns or a stronger magnet: a larger deflection. Reversing the pole: the deflection changes direction.

sections.enonce_markdown: A step-down transformer has $1100$ turns on its primary coil, which is connected to the $220\,\mathrm{V}$ a.c. mains, and $50$ turns on its secondary coil. (a) Calculate the output voltage. (b) The secondary supplies a current of $2.2\,\mathrm{A}$ to a lamp. Calculate the output power and, for an ideal transformer, the primary current. (c) In practice the primary current is $0.125\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the efficiency.

etapes.action: Use the turns ratio to find $V_s$.

etapes.justification: Power is $P = IV$ for the secondary circuit.
An ideal transformer has $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$, so $I_p = P_{out}/V_p$.
The real input power is $V_pI_p$ with the measured current.
Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The output is $10\,\mathrm{V}$ and $22\,\mathrm{W}$. An ideal transformer would draw $0.10\,\mathrm{A}$ in the primary; the real one, drawing $0.125\,\mathrm{A}$, has an efficiency of $80\%$ and the lost power ($5.5\,\mathrm{W}$) heats the core and the coils.

items.erreur_markdown: A transformer can be used with a battery (d.c.) to raise the voltage.
items.pourquoi_faux: With d.c., the magnetic field in the core is constant, so no e.m.f. is induced in the secondary. Only a changing field induces an e.m.f.
items.correction_markdown: A transformer needs a.c. in the primary to produce a changing magnetic field.

items.erreur_markdown: A step-up transformer increases both voltage and power.
items.pourquoi_faux: Power cannot be increased: a step-up transformer raises the voltage and lowers the current by the same factor ($V_pI_p = V_sI_s$ for an ideal one).
items.correction_markdown: Voltage goes up, current goes down, power stays the same (or decreases a little because of losses).

items.erreur_markdown: An e.m.f. is induced in a coil when a magnet is held steady inside it.
items.pourquoi_faux: The e.m.f. only appears while the magnetic field linking the coil is changing, that is, while the magnet is moving relative to the coil.
items.correction_markdown: No relative motion means no change of flux and no e.m.f.

items.erreur_markdown: By Lenz's law the induced current helps the motion of the magnet.
items.pourquoi_faux: The induced current always opposes the change that creates it. If it helped, the magnet would speed up and energy would be created from nothing.
items.correction_markdown: The coil end facing an approaching north pole becomes a north pole and repels the magnet.

items.erreur_markdown: The laminated core is used to increase the magnetic field.
items.pourquoi_faux: The lamination is made of thin insulated sheets so that eddy currents cannot flow around in the core and waste energy as heat. The soft iron is what makes the magnetism strong and easy to reverse.
items.correction_markdown: Laminations reduce eddy currents and heating; soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily.

items.enonce_markdown: A transformer has $500$ turns on the primary and $2500$ turns on the secondary. The primary is connected to a $24\,\mathrm{V}$ a.c. supply. Calculate the secondary voltage. Is it a step-up or a step-down transformer?
items.solution_markdown:
Formula: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$

Substitution: $V_s = 24 \times \dfrac{2500}{500} = 24 \times 5$

Result: **$V_s = 120\,\mathrm{V}$**. The secondary voltage is larger, so it is a **step-up transformer**.

items.enonce_markdown: A phone charger contains a transformer with $2000$ turns on the primary and $100$ turns on the secondary. It is connected to a $220\,\mathrm{V}$ a.c. supply. The secondary delivers $1.5\,\mathrm{A}$. Assuming that the transformer is ideal, calculate (a) the secondary voltage, (b) the output power, and (c) the primary current.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $V_s = 220 \times \dfrac{100}{2000}$, so **$V_s = 11\,\mathrm{V}$**.

(b) $P = V_sI_s = 11 \times 1.5$, so **$P = 16.5\,\mathrm{W}$**.

(c) For an ideal transformer, $V_pI_p = 16.5$, so $I_p = \dfrac{16.5}{220}$, which is **$I_p = 0.075\,\mathrm{A}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed quickly into a coil connected to a sensitive galvanometer. Describe what is observed, state the polarity induced at the end of the coil nearest the magnet, and say what happens if the magnet is pushed in more slowly. (b) A power station sends $50\,\mathrm{kW}$ along cables of total resistance $2.0\,\Omega$. Compare the power wasted in the cables when the transmission voltage is $5000\,\mathrm{V}$ and when it is $500\,\mathrm{V}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The galvanometer needle deflects while the magnet is moving and returns to zero when it stops. The end of the coil nearest the magnet becomes a **north pole**, to repel the approaching magnet (Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change). If the magnet moves more slowly, the field changes more slowly and the deflection is **smaller**.

(b) At $5000\,\mathrm{V}$: $I = \dfrac{50\,000}{5000} = 10\,\mathrm{A}$, and the loss is $I^2R = 10^2 \times 2.0 = 200\,\mathrm{W}$, which is **0.4%** of $50\,\mathrm{kW}$.

At $500\,\mathrm{V}$: $I = \dfrac{50\,000}{500} = 100\,\mathrm{A}$, and the loss is $100^2 \times 2.0 = 20\,000\,\mathrm{W}$, which is **40%** of $50\,\mathrm{kW}$.

Lowering the voltage by a factor of 10 multiplies the loss by 100, so a high voltage must be used.

items_markdown: An e.m.f. is induced when the magnetic field linking a conductor **changes**; it is larger for faster motion, a stronger magnet and more turns (Faraday).
**Lenz's law:** the induced current opposes the change that produces it (conservation of energy).
Transformer: $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$; ideal: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$; it works only with **a.c.**
The core is **soft iron** (easily magnetised and demagnetised) and **laminated** (to reduce eddy currents).
Power is transmitted at **high voltage**, so the current is small and the loss $I^2R$ in the cables is small; a.c. allows this because transformers can step the voltage up and down.
